Focus on sizing reserved GPUs for a latency-sensitive inference workload, tenant isolation and VPC/KMS constraints, and burst/prewarm strategy for unpredictable traffic spikes. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Dana (CTO), Marcus (Head of Platform), Priya (Security)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and Ravi is our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Dana: Good thanks, ready to dig in. We've been noodling on dedicated capacity for a bit.
[00:10] Marcus: Yeah, thanks. We want to validate if reserving capacity makes sense vs staying hosted. Cost, isolation, and burst handling are the big things.
[00:15] Ravi: Great, that's exactly what we want to cover. Before we dig into numbers, can you describe your workload shape and SLOs?
[00:22] Dana: Sure. We're running multimodal inference, mostly text+small images. Latency target is p95 <= 250ms for short responses, about 800ms for larger multimodal prompts. Peak concurrency is spiky — we see 6x baseline for 10-20 minute windows, a few times a day.
[00:40] Marcus: Also, we need tenant-level isolation — we host models for different customers and cannot have noisy-neighbor interference.
[00:46] Priya: And security: keys managed in our KMS (CloudVault), we need CMKs rotated every 90 days, HSM-backed. Also SOC 2 and incident logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:58] Maya: Perfect. A couple of clarifying Qs — what GPU types are you currently using or prefer? And what's your expected qps baseline?
[01:06] Dana: Baseline is about 80 qps, mostly small tokens. For heavy multimodal batches, baseline is 20 qps. For GPUs, we're testing A100s in our infra but open to Ampere and L40 options.
[01:20] Ravi: Makes sense. On Redwood Dedicated we can reserve pools with A100/L40 equivalents; we provide pre-warm and hot-pool patterns to reduce cold start latency. For the spikes you described, our hot-pool prewarmed nodes can absorb short 6x bursts without queueing if sized properly.
[01:38] Marcus: How does prewarm work? Is it a fixed hot pool or dynamic? And what about eviction if capacity is constrained?
[01:44] Ravi: Two pieces — reserved hot pool (customers reserve N nodes kept warmed) and burst to shared capacity where we have fallbacks. For Dedicated customers you can configure a hard isolation policy where only your tenants use the reserved pool — that's strict and avoids noisy neighbors. Eviction policies are configurable; we can opt for graceful preemption with per-request fallback to a cheaper model variant (lower precision / quantized) or to hosted fallback if you permit.
[02:06] Priya: Fallback to hosted is tricky for us because of data residency and compliance. We'd prefer model-variant fallback inside the private/dedicated environment.
[02:12] Ravi: Understood — for Private+Dedicated we can provide variant-based fallbacks within your VPC or on-prem nodes; that doesn't send data out.
[02:20] Dana: Good. On sizing, how do we translate 80 qps baseline with those spikes into node counts?
[02:25] Ravi: We'll run a benchmark pilot, but high-level rule: estimate token-per-second and latency per model. For your short responses on A100-equivalents, one node can often handle 120-200 concurrent small requests depending on batching. With your baseline 80 qps, i'd recommend reserving a modest pool to cover baseline plus safety — say 2-3 reserved nodes — and a hot-pool of 1-2 additional prewarmed nodes for spikes. Then add burst capacity policy for short 6x events.
[02:54] Marcus: That sounds lower than I expected — worried about tail latency when concurrency aligns. How do you handle KV cache warmup for large context windows?
[03:03] Ravi: Good point. We maintain per-request KV caches; warm pool nodes keep common prefixes cached if you have predictable patterns. If your workload has lots of cold prefixes we can do prefix caching at the routing layer or use model sharding rules. Also we can do continuous batching to maximize throughput while honoring latency SLOs.
[03:20] Dana: Ok. Let's talk about KMS — Priya, can you outline constraints?
[03:24] Priya: We require customer-managed keys; CMKs are in CloudVault with HSM. Keys rotate every 90 days and must not be exportable. We need audit logs for every decryption event and key access.
[03:36] Maya: Redwood supports external KMS integration for Dedicated and Private. We store encrypted model weights and data at rest with envelope encryption. Decryption is performed inside the VPC nodes; Redwood can push logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3 sink.
[03:47] Priya: How do you handle key rotation without disrupting active KV caches or models loaded in GPU memory?
[03:52] Ravi: We support a graceful rotation flow: new key versions are staged, nodes fetch new key material for new decrypts, and we maintain previous key for existing runtime instances until restart or redeploy. For model weights already loaded into GPU memory, rotation requires re-encrypt/reload which can be scheduled during maintenance windows. We can also support rolling reloads to minimize disruption.
[04:10] Marcus: What's the expected downtime for a rolling reload on, say, a 10-node pool?
[04:14] Ravi: With staged rolling reload and hot-pool overlap, typical user-visible impact is minimal — a small fraction of requests may go to slightly slower tails, but we can keep p95 within your SLO with careful orchestration. We'll simulate in the benchmark.
[04:28] Dana: On cost, can you give an example pricing shape for reserved nodes + burst?
[04:33] Maya: We'll send exact pricing but high level: reserved commitment (monthly) gives a discount over on-demand, burst usage billed at a premium rate per hour or per-GB-hour. We also have prewarm node flat fees for nodes kept in hot-pools. We'll include a surge matrix showing blended unit cost at different utilization.
[04:47] Marcus: Competitor question — CloudX AI told us they guarantee no preemptions but higher baseline price. Any differences in SLA?
[04:53] Maya: Our Dedicated SLA includes uptime and latency targets for reserved pools; preemption can be configured off for strict isolation. The key difference is we provide routing policies for model-variant fallback and observable token-level costs; competitors may lock you into single fallback options.
[05:08] Priya: We need to see your SOC/ISO docs and a short architecture diagram showing where keys live.
[05:12] Maya: We'll share the security whitepaper and an architecture sketch — I'll attach links. Also we'll include the KMS integration guide.
[05:20] Marcus: Pilot — we want a 24-72 hour benchmark using our sample traffic (we'll anonymize). What do you need?
[05:26] Ravi: We'll need a representative prompt set, a short load script, and an expected SLAs doc. We'll spin a pilot cluster inside your VPC or Redwood-managed dedicated with VPC peering depending on the path you choose. For fastest results, Redwood-managed Dedicated with VPC peering is easiest.
[05:40] Dana: We prefer self-hosted nodes in our VPC for compliance but open to Redwood-managed for speed.
[05:45] Maya: We can offer both. Next step is to scope the pilot and dates. Any timeline constraints?
[05:50] Dana: We'd like pilot next week if possible, contract by end of month.
[05:54] Maya: Okay, we'll prioritize.
[05:56] Priya: One more — network egress rules: if we use Redwood-managed, can you guarantee no data egress outside our region and provide IP allowlist?
[06:03] Ravi: Yes, regional isolation and static egress IPs available for dedicated customers. We'll include the IP ranges and routing doc.
[06:10] Marcus: For observability, does Redwood provide token-level cost breakout and per-route latency dashboards?
[06:15] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-model latency heatmaps, traces and per-route dashboards. We can also push traces to your tracing endpoint.
[06:24] Marcus: Great. I want to avoid noisy neighbor problems — is physical tenancy available?
[06:29] Ravi: For the strictest isolation needs we offer single-tenant physical nodes as part of Private deployments — that's more expensive but gives full hardware isolation. For most customers, reserved pools with strict scheduling and tenant fencing suffices.
[06:42] Dana: Alright, recap?
[06:44] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pricing + security docs + KMS guide; Ravi to draft pilot plan and required artifacts; Quantum Harbor to provide sample prompts, load script, and KMS constraints. Pilot targeted next week, contract by month-end.
[06:58] Dana: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:01] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with links.
[07:05] End meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels may be generic and a few product names mis-transcribed (e.g. "CloudVault" might be "CloudVault/CloudVault-KMS") and timings are approximate. References: redwood-dedicated-specs.pdf (shared), redwood-kms-integration.md (shared), pilot-benchmark-template.xlsx (shared).
